S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor occurring within three months of the onset of that stressor. The reaction is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor, considering cultural and contextual factors, and is associated with significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Symptoms do not meet criteria for another specific mental disorder and do not represent normal bereavement, and once the stressor or its consequences have resolved, the disturbance typically does not persist for more than an additional six months. Clinically it is often seen in the context of life transitions, interpersonal conflict, medical illness, or occupational stress, and is distinguished from other disorders by its clear temporal and causal relationship to a discrete stressor and its relatively time‑limited course.

patient.personality: Richard is a highly disciplined, competitive, and sociable planner who thrives on structure, precision projects, and being seen as the dependable organizer in both work and community life.
patient.stressor: About six months ago, Richard’s plant underwent a major restructuring after losing a major contract, and he was promoted to senior production planner while simultaneously being asked to manage with fewer staff and tighter deadlines. Initially he treated it as a challenge, pouring himself into reworking schedules and volunteering for every cross‑functional meeting, but the constant pressure, late nights, and blame for any bottleneck began to erode the sense of control he usually maintains over his life. Over the following five months, the strain spilled over into his hobbies and social routines—he started skipping basketball games, putting off woodworking projects, and becoming increasingly tense and irritable at the fire hall, while feeling unable to “switch off” from work. When his plant manager informally warned him about recent mistakes and a close friend at the range commented that he seemed like a “different person,” Richard reluctantly agreed to see a psychiatrist at the urging of his sister, recognizing that his response to the job changes was starting to derail both his performance and his relationships.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since all the changes at the plant, I feel like I’m not handling the stress right and it’s starting to mess up my work and everything else.”

S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.
S081.manifestation: Ever since the promotion and the plant shake-up, it’s like my whole life has turned into one big deadline I can’t meet—I'm snapping at guys over tiny scheduling errors, lying awake replaying production charts in my head, skipping basketball and the fire hall because I feel too keyed up and worn down at the same time, and even small things like my wife asking what’s for dinner can set me off or make me want to just shut down and be left alone.
